articles.summary_ja: Pytorchの教科書としては非常に詳細で、実践的な方法を提示しています。

articles.title: Toward a theory of Evaluability
articles.summary: Machine learning models, particularly large foundation models, are increasingly evaluated along multiple axes that are relevant for their usage. In addition to accuracy measures appropriate for the…
articles.abstract: Machine learning models, particularly large foundation models, are increasingly evaluated along multiple axes that are relevant for their usage. In addition to accuracy measures appropriate for the specific task of interest, measures capturing safety, calibration and fairness properties are often of interest. The classical approach to these problems assumes that the test set has been held out from the training process, an assumption that is increasingly harder to justify for large foundation models. In this work, we formalize a notion of evaluability without this assumption, and ask if it is feasible to evaluate black-box models in settings where our test samples may have been used during training. We study this problem under different settings, capturing different levels of access to the model. We first study the natural setting, where the evaluator only looks at the output of the model on the test set. We fully characterize the class of distributions where accurate evaluation is possible, and show tight upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity of evaluation. Our results show that black-box evaluation in this setup is feasible if and only if the distribution is close to being small support. We then consider evaluation algorithms that can query the model on additional inputs and demonstrate connections to self-correctors studied in program testing. Using these, we show that a small amount of query access can increase the power of the evaluator for natural distributions and concept classes.

articles.title: JUBILEE: A Benchmark Environment for Off-Policy Evaluation in Debt Collections
articles.summary: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value a candidate decision policy would achieve, using only data logged by the policy already in production. In debt collections, unrecorded factors can…
articles.abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value a candidate decision policy would achieve, using only data logged by the policy already in production. In debt collections, unrecorded factors can influence both actions and outcomes. This paper presents JUBILEE, a benchmark environment built around a debt-collections simulator that generates million-loan panels with competing risks, rare recovery events, and hidden factors driving both outcomes and assignment. The evaluation includes an 80-run comparison of tabular and gradient-boosted estimators under two synthetic outcome mechanisms and a 190-run parameter grid. Independent policy simulations provide reference values with estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty for a synthetic reward score and for simulated cash. With hidden factors influencing action assignment, several tabular methods agree closely while underestimating the field-visit policy's score, an error that also appears with boosted models. Intervals from tabular doubly robust estimation usually contain the reference without hidden assignment dependence but mostly miss it when that dependence is present. Estimates from randomized decisions do not show the same large error, although their limited precision leaves policy choice uncertain. The decision consequences depend on how policy value is defined. The field-visit policy ranks last under the score and first under simulated cash, which excludes channel costs. Under cash, log-based estimators miss this best candidate in nearly every run with hidden assignment dependence in the paired study. JUBILEE supports reproducible study of these failure modes under specified collections mechanisms.

articles.title: Bayesian transfer for offline Q-learning with multi-task Gaussian processes
articles.summary: Offline reinforcement learning can benefit from data collected in related tasks, yet indiscriminate knowledge transfer may lead to negative transfer under task mismatch and limited target-data…
articles.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning can benefit from data collected in related tasks, yet indiscriminate knowledge transfer may lead to negative transfer under task mismatch and limited target-data coverage. We propose a target-aware Bayesian transfer framework for offline Q-learning based on multi-task Gaussian processes that jointly model task-specific Q-functions. Source tasks are assessed using target predictive evidence and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), while posterior uncertainty and behavior-supported action sets guide conservative Bellman updates and policy extraction. To account for the dependence induced by Bellman bootstrapping, we distinguish Bellman innovations from bootstrap errors and establish stability and predictive source-selection results under explicit regularity conditions. We further derive selection-adaptive posterior contraction and offline policy-performance bounds, identifying the structural conditions under which source information can be pooled to achieve minimax-optimal rates in a shared-function Gaussian sequence experiment. Simulation studies with heterogeneous source tasks demonstrate improved target Q-function estimation and reduced material negative transfer compared with indiscriminate source pooling. An application to human decision-making data further shows higher average expected immediate payoff than both target-only learning and matched-size random source selection. These results highlight the benefits of combining target-aware source selection with uncertainty-aware conservative learning for reliable and sample-efficient offline reinforcement learning.

articles.title: Causal Outcome Learning with Noisy Proxies
articles.summary: Modern observational biomedical datasets contain increasingly extensive baseline and outcome measurements, yet detecting a clinically meaningful treatment effect remains difficult because…
articles.abstract: Modern observational biomedical datasets contain increasingly extensive baseline and outcome measurements, yet detecting a clinically meaningful treatment effect remains difficult because investigators must identify an outcome that captures treatment response while adjusting for confounding distributed across numerous noisy baseline variables. We introduce SCOUT (Score-based Causal Outcome Learning Using Treatment signals), a framework that learns a clinically interpretable, treatment-responsive outcome while adjusting for confounding throughout the learning process. SCOUT constructs low-dimensional adjustment representations of high-dimensional baseline measurements to estimate the average treatment effect (ATE) and conditional average treatment effect (CATE) for the learned outcome. Importantly, the final adjustment space is at most two-dimensional, allowing treatment-effect heterogeneity to be estimated in this space rather than in the full high-dimensional covariate space. SCOUT also introduces a fourth-order statistic for testing treatment-effect heterogeneity that emphasizes unusually large deviations from the ATE. In synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments, the algorithm achieved competitive ATE estimation accuracy and substantially lower CATE estimation error. In an observational study of patients with bipolar disorder, SCOUT identified a clinically recognizable lithium-associated adverse-effect profile, detecting both a significant ATE (Holm-adjusted $p$ = 0.0026) and significant treatment-effect heterogeneity (Holm-adjusted $p$ = 0.033).These results demonstrate how jointly learning outcomes and controlling for confounding can facilitate the discovery of treatment effects in high-dimensional observational data.

articles.title: Prescriptive Learning of Linear Policies with Feasibility Guarantees for Binary Decision-Making
articles.summary: Binary decision-making under uncertainty arises across a wide range of applications, including energy systems scheduling, transportation, and workforce planning. While machine learning has been…
articles.abstract: Binary decision-making under uncertainty arises across a wide range of applications, including energy systems scheduling, transportation, and workforce planning. While machine learning has been increasingly applied to accelerate or replace mixed-integer solvers in such settings, existing approaches rely on predictive learning, training models to reproduce optimal decisions from labeled data, which lacks knowledge of counterfactual outcomes and provides no guarantees that the resulting decisions will be feasible. This limitation is further compounded under distributional shift, where policies trained on historical data may produce systematically infeasible decisions. We propose a prescriptive learning framework for binary decision-making that addresses both limitations. Rather than predicting optimal labels, the framework jointly optimizes over linear decision policies and feasible assignments across all training scenarios, allowing feasible alternatives and their operational performance to be considered directly during training. We further extend the framework to a distributionally robust chance-constrained formulation using a Wasserstein ambiguity set, which enforces feasibility with a prescribed probability under the worst-case distribution in the ambiguity set and enables a tunable trade-off between robustness and solution quality. We demonstrate the framework on two case studies, namely a unit commitment problem and a staff allocation problem. Out-of-sample experiments under test distributions that either match or differ from the training distribution show that the robust model is more conservative when the two distributions coincide, while under distributional shift it substantially reduces unmet demand and lowers total cost by up to 76.5% relative to classical predictive learning.

articles.title: Robust Satisficing Ensemble: Scalable Model Aggregation Under Distribution Shifts
articles.summary: Standard ensemble methods can improve robustness by mitigating individual model stochasticity, but they frequently fail to generalize beyond the training distribution, leaving systems vulnerable to…
articles.abstract: Standard ensemble methods can improve robustness by mitigating individual model stochasticity, but they frequently fail to generalize beyond the training distribution, leaving systems vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. We introduce the Robust Satisficing Ensemble (RSE), a scalable probabilistic aggregation framework designed to secure model combinations by minimizing their fragility against distributional changes. By bridging a robust satisficing objective with a quadratic risk surrogate, RSE derives an analytical inner adversary. This fundamental reformulation enables highly efficient weight updates without the computational bottleneck of standard minimax optimization, crucially decoupling optimization complexity from sample size to scale effectively to large datasets. In particular, we prove a geometrically decaying truncation error for the fragility approximation via Lagrange-Burmann expansion and establish stationarity guarantees for RSE. We evaluate RSE across a comprehensive spectrum of distribution shifts, including adversarial label shift (SST-5, TREC), natural subpopulation and temporal shifts (CivilComments, HuffPost). Our results demonstrate that RSE consistently outperforms strong robust baselines, including GroupDRO, IRM, and SRM. These findings establish RSE as a practical, theoretically grounded safeguard for reliable model aggregation in dynamic environments.

articles.title: On Generalization in Bilevel Least Squares with Overparameterized Neural Networks
articles.summary: Bilevel optimization addresses machine learning problems in which the outer objective is a value function implicitly defined through the solution of an inner problem. While its algorithmic aspects…
articles.abstract: Bilevel optimization addresses machine learning problems in which the outer objective is a value function implicitly defined through the solution of an inner problem. While its algorithmic aspects are well developed, its generalization properties remain much less understood. In this paper, we study the generalization of inexact gradient methods when both objectives are least-squares regression problems and when the estimator of the value function's gradient, or hypergradient, is obtained by implicit differentiation in function space. This approach allows us to derive stationarity bounds for these methods in terms of the uniform generalization errors of the two regression functions needed to estimate the hypergradient. When these regression functions are defined as overparameterized two-layer ReLU networks trained by gradient flow with early stopping, we obtain explicit finite-sample bounds on these generalization errors in the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime. Combining these with our general inexact gradient analysis shows the effect of sample size on the overall convergence of the bilevel method. Numerical experiments on synthetic data illustrate our results. Beyond the NTK regime, further experiments reveal an initialization-dependent implicit bias induced by the bilevel structure, which can lead to feature learning at the inner level and overall performance improvements.

articles.title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement with Statistical Guarantees
articles.summary: Recursive self-improvement offers a promising path toward AI agents that improve through experience by refining their own harnesses without retraining their underlying large language models (LLMs).…
articles.abstract: Recursive self-improvement offers a promising path toward AI agents that improve through experience by refining their own harnesses without retraining their underlying large language models (LLMs). Making this self-improvement process reliable, however, requires more than generating new updates: agents must decide which changes are worth keeping. A greedy gate that accepts updates based solely on higher validation scores can mistake an observed gain for genuine progress and lead to performance degeneration, whereas overly conservative statistical gates may reject beneficial updates and hinder performance improvement. We introduce Trustworthy Recursive Updates with Statistical Testing (TRUST), a framework that adapts an online multiple hypothesis testing procedure to control the rate of false evolution across rounds, with an LLM analyzing historical context to help determine how much evidence is required to update the incumbent. Under interpretable assumptions, we prove that TRUST limits the proportion of accepted updates that result in unacceptable performance loss. We further derive a lower bound on the final performance gain. Across the benchmarks HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS with the models DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.8-Flash, TRUST reduces the average ratio of accepted inferior updates from the greedy gate's 45.59% to 2.78%, while achieving higher final scores than the state-of-the-art statistical gate baselines for recursive self-improvement. These findings demonstrate that TRUST strikes a balance between statistical reliability and performance gain in recursive self-improvement.

articles.title: Matchability-Aware Conformal Prediction for Open-Ended Language Model Generation
articles.summary: Large language models (LLMs) often do not produce calibrated uncertainty estimates for their answers. We propose CAELUM, a framework that builds semantic prediction sets while separating aleatoric…
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often do not produce calibrated uncertainty estimates for their answers. We propose CAELUM, a framework that builds semantic prediction sets while separating aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty. CAELUM samples answers using an ensemble of clarification prompts, clusters them by semantic equivalence, and estimates the aleatoric and epistemic components via kernel-based von Neumann entropy before calibrating nonconformity scores with split conformal prediction. We use a weight $w_λ(x)=1+U_{\mathrm{ale}}(x)+λ\,U_{\mathrm{epi}}(x)$ to control for the contribution of the epistemic uncertainty of each instance and fit a coefficient $λ^\star$ to minimize prediction set size. When the objective is nonflat and selection is stable across splits, $λ^\star$ could be a diagnostic, where large values may indicate epistemic dominance (retrieve, abstain) and $λ^\star\to 0$ aleatoric dominance (clarify). For individual queries, a log ratio $R(x)$ compares the weighted epistemic component with the aleatoric component. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the coverage is capped by matchability, the fraction of items whose reference answer appears in any sampled cluster. Empirically, this matchability can be predicted from the original question features using a lightweight classifier. We use those predictions to define a stratum and derive a conformal coverage bound within it. Across 30 LLM and dataset combinations (4-32B), mean coverage is 0.74 in the learned stratum versus 0.65 overall, averaged over the 78 evaluations using the learned classifier. Project page: https://unco3892.github.io/caelum/

articles.title: A Geometric Theory for Nonequilibrium Transformer Dynamics
articles.summary: We develop a variational and geometric theory based on statistical physics for the joint evolution of Transformer attention and token representations at fixed model parameters. To this end, we…
articles.abstract: We develop a variational and geometric theory based on statistical physics for the joint evolution of Transformer attention and token representations at fixed model parameters. To this end, we introduce a free energy for the attention and model the evolution of the attention weights by its Fisher--Rao gradient flow. At fixed token representations, we prove that the softmax matrix is the unique free-energy minimiser and that every positive attention trajectory converges to it. For prescribed time-dependent representations, we show that the attention dynamics becomes linear after a change to logit variables. This result yields tracking bounds relative to the instantaneous softmax and sufficient conditions for attention to converge to a fixed matrix. Hamiltonian dynamics for the representations and their momenta are then coupled to the attention relaxation driven by the same energy. This coupling results in an energy-dissipation law. We also develop two alternative Hamiltonians incorporating the attention value map. We prove global well-posedness of the attention flow and all three coupled systems.

articles.title: Deep backward multistep high-order regression methods for high dimensional nonlinear parabolic partial differential equations
articles.summary: We propose a deep backward multistep high-order regression (MHDBR) method for semilinear parabolic partial differential equations through their backward stochastic differential equation…
articles.abstract: We propose a deep backward multistep high-order regression (MHDBR) method for semilinear parabolic partial differential equations through their backward stochastic differential equation representations. The method combines multistep time discretization with regression targets formed by conditional expectations. Under explicit regularity, starting-value, forward-approximation and network-moment assumptions, we prove an error bound separating time discretization, conditional Monte Carlo sampling and neural-network approximation. The analysis assumes exact population minimization; finite-training-sample generalization and optimization errors are not included. For generators independent of the gradient variable, suitably constrained GroupSort networks and sufficiently large conditional sample sizes give order $J$ in the stated nodal $L^2$ error norm. The required network sizes depend on dimension, so this result does not establish dimension-independent complexity. We present a reproducible time-discretization test satisfying the analytical assumptions and three broader neural-network benchmarks, whose relation to the assumptions is discussed explicitly.

articles.title: Confronting Uncertainty in Mechanism-AI Coupled Dynamical Systems via Optimal Transport and Information Geometry: Part I. Distribution Learning
articles.summary: Mechanism-AI coupled dynamical systems are increasingly used to study complex biological systems. However, uncertainty associated with noisy, sparse, and partially observed data limits their…
articles.abstract: Mechanism-AI coupled dynamical systems are increasingly used to study complex biological systems. However, uncertainty associated with noisy, sparse, and partially observed data limits their reliability. This paper presents a systematic mathematical formulation for treating these uncertainties from the perspective of optimal transport and information geometry. We formulate the uncertainty quantification problem as the minimization of an energy functional on a probability density space equipped with a Riemannian metric, with the loss evaluated through a differential equation, and give a unified description of the gradient flows of the energy functional under specific metrics, such as the Wasserstein and Fisher-Rao metrics. Furthermore, we present corresponding numerical methods for solving these gradient flows using abstract adjoint sensitivity analysis. The formulation connects a range of Bayesian inference methods for dynamical systems; numerical experiments compare posterior approximation and predictive uncertainty under a common computational budget. Moreover, it also provides a geometric perspective on dynamical modeling and the study of heterogeneity evolution.

articles.title: Close and Sort: Exact Maximum-Likelihood Aggregation of Cyclic Rank-Two Preferences
articles.summary: Pairwise probabilities arise in rank aggregation, recommendation, and human or LLM evaluation, yet converting them into a maximum-likelihood list is a weighted Kemeny problem and is NP-hard in…
articles.abstract: Pairwise probabilities arise in rank aggregation, recommendation, and human or LLM evaluation, yet converting them into a maximum-likelihood list is a weighted Kemeny problem and is NP-hard in general. Known exact algorithms for rank-two tournaments use only comparison signs and do not optimize this likelihood. We show that the weighted problem is exactly solvable when the skew-symmetric log-odds matrix $W_{ij}=\log(p_{ij}/p_{ji})$ has rank two, including when the induced preferences contain cycles. Writing $W_{ij}=\det(h_i,h_j)$ and adding the closing vector $h_0=-\sum_i h_i$ turns the objective into twice the signed area of a closed polygon. This geometry yields CloseSort, which polar-sorts the $n+1$ edge vectors, cuts after $h_0$, and returns a global maximum-likelihood order in $O(n\log n)$ time from the factors. The same geometry identifies the runner-up and gives a stability certificate beyond exact rank two. When the smallest determinant $δ$ of two consecutive edges in the closed angular cycle is positive, it is exactly the best-to-runner-up log-likelihood gap. For $W=W_0+E$, the CloseSort order of $W_0$ has regret at most $\sum_{i<j}|E_{ij}|$ on $W$ and remains optimal whenever this sum is below $δ$, a worst-case tight threshold. In 5,120 determinant-logit simulations, increasing the observations per pair from 4 to 64 raises the fraction on which rank-two projection outperforms the empirical plug-in optimum from 68.6% to 85.7%. On 3,600 Arena-Hard LLM-judge profiles drawn from 63 systems and ten judges, the leading rank-two component captures 89.2% of the log-odds energy. On profiles containing a directed majority triangle, CloseSort reduces normalized regret by 44% relative to Borda and improves the mean normalized objective over each of eight baselines. With factors supplied, it is 8,407 times faster than exact dynamic programming on 18-item rankings.

articles.title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series
articles.summary: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and…
articles.abstract: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without a single annotation, language model call, or domain expert. Code is available at: https://github.com/Sachithx/ConceptTime.git.

articles.title: Group-Conditional Conformal Risk Control: Exact Guarantees, Limits, and Overlapping Extensions
articles.summary: We study group-conditional conformal risk control (CRC) for disjoint and overlapping groups under bounded monotone losses. For disjoint groups, we establish exact finite-sample conditional risk…
articles.abstract: We study group-conditional conformal risk control (CRC) for disjoint and overlapping groups under bounded monotone losses. For disjoint groups, we establish exact finite-sample conditional risk control, two-sided bounds on the group-restricted risk, and fundamental limitations arising from local support and calibration-rank granularity. For overlapping groups, we study two exactly valid approaches: group-restricted calibration followed by union deployment, and direct calibration of the deployed prediction-set family. We characterize the union's limiting reconciliation gap, identify conditions for its disappearance, and establish sharp lower bounds for structured losses in specified product-form models. We also demonstrate a strict size advantage for direct calibration in an ordinal model. Experiments show that direct calibration can reduce prediction-set size, but its efficiency depends on group structure, loss type, and shape fitting. Results on historical diabetic-retinopathy scores further illustrate these tradeoffs. Overall, local support, reconciliation slack, and threshold heterogeneity determine efficiency, with neither approach uniformly dominating.

articles.title: Beyond Discrete Ancestry Groups: Distribution-Aware In-Context Learning for Cancer Outcome Prediction Across the Genetic Ancestry Continuum
articles.summary: Machine learning models for omics-based prediction of cancer outcomes are commonly built on aggregated data without distinguishing ancestry groups, or under an ancestry-discrete design, which…
articles.abstract: Machine learning models for omics-based prediction of cancer outcomes are commonly built on aggregated data without distinguishing ancestry groups, or under an ancestry-discrete design, which partitions samples into ancestry groups and fits a separate model within each group. Recent evidence shows that this approach is inherently limited: predictive accuracy declines with genetic distance from the training samples, even within a single ancestry group, because the data distribution shifts continuously rather than only between predefined categories. In this paper, we propose distribution-aware in-context learning (DA-ICL) for ancestry-continuum modeling. Our method extends conventional ancestry-discrete modeling to ancestry-continuum modeling, capturing the nonstationary omics-endpoint relationship across the genetic continuum while enabling efficient modeling through an in-context learning foundation model. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating the superiority of the ancestry-continuum over ancestry-discrete modeling, along with empirical results supporting the proposed framework. Source code is available at https://github.com/ai4pm/DA-ICL-Continuum.

articles.title: Zeroth-Order Langevin Dynamics for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization: Curvature Regularization and Non-Asymptotic Guarantees
articles.summary: Zeroth-order methods provide a way to optimize stochastic nonconvex objectives using only noisy function evaluations. However, the smoothing inherent in their gradient estimators effectively modifies…
articles.abstract: Zeroth-order methods provide a way to optimize stochastic nonconvex objectives using only noisy function evaluations. However, the smoothing inherent in their gradient estimators effectively modifies the objective being optimized. In particular, Gaussian smoothing with smoothing parameter $η>0$ induces, to leading order, an implicit Hessian-trace regularization, which motivates the study of the curvature-regularized objective of the form $f(x)+(η^2/2) tr(\nabla^2 f(x))$. We develop a non-asymptotic theory in the nonconvex setting for a class of algorithms called stochastic zeroth-order Langevin dynamics (ZOLD), which use only noisy function evaluations and do not have access to first- or higher-order derivative information, and derive excess-risk guarantees for the curvature-regularized objective. We first control the finite-time distribution of the ZOLD iterates in Wasserstein distance with respect to the Gibbs measure associated with the Gaussian-smoothed objective. An explicit coupling between the smoothing and inverse temperature parameters then quantifies the proximity of this measure to the Gibbs measure associated with the corresponding Hessian-trace-regularized objective. These distributional estimates in Wasserstein distance lead to excess-risk bounds for the curvature-regularized objective. Our analysis accommodates assumptions under which the stochastic function evaluations are allowed to have non-uniform dependence on the data stream. In addition, the constants in the non-asymptotic bounds do not rely on log-Sobolev or Poincaré inequalities as in prior zeroth-order Langevin analyses. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first non-asymptotic analysis of a zeroth-order Langevin method that simultaneously establishes excess-risk guarantees for a curvature-regularized objective and Wasserstein guarantees for the associated Gibbs measure in the nonconvex setting.

articles.title: Causal Discovery Grounding and the Naturalness Assumption
articles.summary: Standard causal discovery postulates that structure can be described by a directed acyclic graph (DAG), which can be partially reconstructed by using the faithfulness principle. According to this…
articles.abstract: Standard causal discovery postulates that structure can be described by a directed acyclic graph (DAG), which can be partially reconstructed by using the faithfulness principle. According to this principle, conditional independencies in the observational distribution correspond exactly to those encoded in the unknown DAG. However, such algorithms are challenged by the fact that, without even stronger assumptions, approximate failures of faithfulness are empirically undistinguishable from exact ones. This leaves an inferential gap which can lead to major implications to causal effect identification. We introduce a different perspective, not reliant on exact independencies. By considering the specialized problem of discovering whether unmeasured confounding can be ruled out for a particular cause-effect pair, we introduce a principle we call naturalness, in which the strength of observational associations bounds the strength of causal dependencies. The bounding function is unknown, with degrees of freedom not present in faithfulness. We model uncertainty about this function using a Bayesian framing which allows for the use of experiments from separate studies, grounding an adaptive causal discovery principle on historical experimental data. We demonstrate its usefulness in partial identification of causal effects, and discuss how the promising results can motivate new principles for general causal discovery.

articles.title: SAMBoost: Spatially Aware Mesh Boosting
articles.summary: We propose SAMBoost (Spatially Aware Mesh Boosting), a gradient boosting method that combines tree-based covariate modelling with a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) latent spatial…
articles.abstract: We propose SAMBoost (Spatially Aware Mesh Boosting), a gradient boosting method that combines tree-based covariate modelling with a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) latent spatial field through a single penalised objective. At each boosting iteration, the predictor is decomposed into separate covariate and spatial components. The method is motivated by applications in which the spatial effect is not a nuisance to be removed but a quantity of interest that must be recovered alongside the covariates. In insurance, for example, practitioners need both flexible nonlinear covariate effects and an interpretable geographic risk surface that can be reported on its own. Existing approaches often involve trade-offs, offering flexible covariate modelling but no explicit spatial field, rigorous spatial inference with a fixed additive covariate structure, or a combination of both at computational costs that limit practicality for large datasets. SAMBoost addresses these goals within the boosting loop, and the underlying mesh produces a sparse precision structure whose cost is largely independent of sample size. On simulations and on an open benchmark, SAMBoost matches or improves on the predictive accuracy of joint Gaussian process and tree boosting approaches. It is also faster and recovers the spatial field and covariate effects more accurately. When covariate effects include interactions, it outperforms additive Bayesian spatial models. Applied to a flood insurance portfolio with 4.9 million records, SAMBoost trains on the full training set without subsampling and runs about sixteen times faster than a Bayesian reference, with a consistent spatial risk surface. A public Python implementation is available.

articles.title: Bias, Measurement Error, and Double-Dipping: When Can GNN Convolutions Help Brain Connectome Prediction?
articles.summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are an important tool for fMRI prediction, where empirical functional connectivity matrices serve both as features and for graph construction. However, recent studies and…
articles.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are an important tool for fMRI prediction, where empirical functional connectivity matrices serve both as features and for graph construction. However, recent studies and our own experiments show that these methods often fail to outperform simpler graph-agnostic baselines. We propose a statistical explanation for this failure by formulating connectome prediction as an errors-in-variables (EIV) problem: the true connectome is latent, while the observed covariance matrix is a noisy finite-time-series estimate. In a linear asymptotic setting, we decompose the effect of graph convolution into three mechanisms: smoothing-induced bias and variance reduction, graph estimation error, and a double-dipping effect arising when the same noisy matrix determines both graph and features. Under a latent community model adapted to neuroscience, we identify a narrow favorable regime, set by the brain community structure, the predictive signal, the graph construction and the recording length, in which message passing can improve prediction. Simulations validate this decomposition, while real-data experiments illustrate that connectome GNN pipelines often fall outside this regime. Our results provide a first step towards explaining when graph convolutions can help brain connectome prediction, and why they often do not.

articles.title: Information-Theoretic Generalization for Set-Input Optimization-Valued Objectives
articles.summary: Modern machine learning is increasingly evaluated using criteria such as multicalibration, CVaR, and Cressie-Read DRO, which target subgroup reliability, tail risk, and distributional robustness…
articles.abstract: Modern machine learning is increasingly evaluated using criteria such as multicalibration, CVaR, and Cressie-Read DRO, which target subgroup reliability, tail risk, and distributional robustness rather than averages of fixed per-example losses. Existing information-theoretic generalization bounds for pointwise losses do not directly apply, because these empirical criteria depend on the entire batch and involve a post-hoc auxiliary optimization over witnesses, thresholds, or reweightings. We formalize this structure as set-input optimization-valued objectives. In the balanced supersample setting, we bound the expected optimized validation-training gap in terms of an objective-dependent sub-Gaussian parameter and the square root of the prediction-based conditional mutual information (fCMI) between the learned supersample prediction table and the selector vector. Combining this with fixed-predictor population-validation comparisons yields unified algorithm-dependent generalization bounds. We verify sub-Gaussianity of the selector gap using stability and convex L2-Lipschitz certificates, obtaining concrete bounds for multicalibration, CVaR, and Cressie-Read DRO, with a stability-based single-index refinement.

articles.title: Spiking Sensory Networks
articles.summary: Effective sensory reception is critical for survival, yet the computational mechanisms behind how peripheral sensory neurons (SNs) transduce external signals into spiking representations for…
articles.abstract: Effective sensory reception is critical for survival, yet the computational mechanisms behind how peripheral sensory neurons (SNs) transduce external signals into spiking representations for downstream brain circuits remain to be fully understood. Numerous theoretical frameworks have been proposed to model sensory processing, with Bayesian approaches among the most prominent. However, existing machine learning attempts to apply Bayesian theory to spiking neurons remain largely phenomenological, disconnected from empirical biology, and poorly validated on non-stationary temporal data. Conversely, neuroscientific models often rely on strong inductive experimental biases or explicit kinetic dynamics fit post hoc to match spiking data. Here, we introduce a class of recurrent Poisson VAE models, termed Spiking Sensory Networks (SSNs), that bridge these paradigms by reconciling variational inference with biologically inspired spike transduction for time-varying stimuli. Evaluated on real-world odor plume recordings from locust olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs), SSNs match or exceed the reconstruction fidelity of Spiking Neural Network (SNN) and GLM baselines while exhibiting superior representational characteristics. Furthermore, SSNs are well-suited for neuroscientific investigation, learning empirical in vivo ORN response motifs and exhibiting emergent spike-frequency adaptation under unsupervised reconstruction without manual tuning. Moreover, we theoretically link the recurrent decoding objective to mutual information maximization, and derive a formal thermodynamic lower bound connecting the Poisson Kullback-Leibler regularizer to the excess non-equilibrium metabolic power of biophysical homeostasis. Ultimately, our work synthesizes principles from machine learning theory and empirical neuroscience, providing a viable bridge that concretizes Bayesian models with biological mechanisms.

articles.title: On the universal structure in deterministic generative diffusion
articles.summary: Diffusion-based generative modeling has emerged as a general computational framework for simulating high-dimensional, structured data across various domains. Understanding its generative mechanisms…
articles.abstract: Diffusion-based generative modeling has emerged as a general computational framework for simulating high-dimensional, structured data across various domains. Understanding its generative mechanisms is paramount for advancing model training and inference in a principled way. Here, we demonstrate that deterministic sampling trajectories share a universal geometric structure invariant to data modalities and diffusion model implementations. This structure can be largely explained by an exactly solvable model based on the optimal linear denoiser.

articles.title: Objective Diversification of Dynamic Hedging
articles.summary: A hedging objective reflects the risk preference of the hedger, so the conventional approach is to estimate the hedge ratio directly under the chosen objective. This paper asks whether that estimate…
articles.abstract: A hedging objective reflects the risk preference of the hedger, so the conventional approach is to estimate the hedge ratio directly under the chosen objective. This paper asks whether that estimate should be used alone. We construct five objective-specific rolling hedge-ratio estimators---minimum variance, least absolute deviation (LAD), downside semivariance, lower-tail quantile, and Expected Shortfall (ES)---from the same historical stock--market returns, and combine the resulting estimates under a fixed final evaluation objective. Separate multi-output ExtraTrees models predict the within-stock-date ranks of the five candidates under MSE, LAD, downside semivariance, and 10\% quantile loss. The design uses pre-specified 60-, 90-, 120-, and 180-day windows with objective-matched rolling estimators as benchmarks. Adaptive weighting improves the corresponding loss in all sixteen objective--window comparisons. Equal weighting, which uses the same objective-specific hedge ratios without state variables or learned reweighting, already improves downside and quantile hedging. The results therefore suggest that estimates generated under other objectives can be useful even when the final hedging preference and evaluation objective are fixed, while adaptive weighting can provide a further improvement.

articles.title: The forces at hand: social learning is permissive, not instructive, for the evolution of phenotypic plasticity
articles.summary: Evolution can favour a trait for two reasons: an instructive cause makes selection favour the trait; a permissive one lets it persist once selection no longer removes it. The distinction matters most…
articles.abstract: Evolution can favour a trait for two reasons: an instructive cause makes selection favour the trait; a permissive one lets it persist once selection no longer removes it. The distinction matters most for phenotypic plasticity and its replacement by inherited behaviour, genetic assimilation, the Baldwin effect. Social learning is credited with favouring plasticity on evidence that cannot tell the two apart: how much plasticity remains at the end of a simulation. Here we show, analytically and computationally, which role it plays in a minimal model of learning and evolution. Writing expected fitness as a function of plasticity, we find that environmental change is the only source of benefit from plasticity, and the social channel enters only its cost. Simulation confirms this: in a static environment selection against plasticity never reverses sign at any channel strength; when the environment changes, it reverses at a threshold the channel lowers, and without the channel the population collapses before reaching it. Social learning is permissive, not instructive: it supplies the means to be plastic, never the reason. For the debate over whether plasticity leads evolution, this is one case settled by measurement: environmental change directs, socially inherited information permits, and neither suffices alone.

articles.title: Winning Reviews, Losing Discovery? The Co-Evolutionary Game of AI Research and Peer Review
articles.summary: Autonomous research systems can produce convincing manuscripts whose scientific value is difficult to verify, while automated reviewers can reward the appearance of completeness. We examine how this…
articles.abstract: Autonomous research systems can produce convincing manuscripts whose scientific value is difficult to verify, while automated reviewers can reward the appearance of completeness. We examine how this gap can become a self-reinforcing threat to the research community. In a two-population evolutionary game, authors choose between acceptance-oriented and exploratory research, and reviewers choose between proxy evaluation and careful assessment. Cheaper acceptance-oriented production can increase review pressure, making proxy assessment more attractive; proxy assessment can in turn strengthen the incentive to produce reviewer-compatible work. We derive conditions under which this feedback sustains a stable regime that rewards publication success while reducing the scientific value of accepted work. An analytical basin boundary explains why the same institutional rules can support either this regime or exploratory research with careful review. Numerical illustrations show how publication counts can conceal scientific loss, how faster adjustment can reinforce existing practices, and why partial reform may fail once the cycle is established. Careful audits and reviewer rewards can reverse the feedback, while temporary support can produce lasting recovery if it moves the community across the basin boundary. The model identifies a warning mechanism rather than forecasting a particular conference: a review system can remain operational and privately rewarding while becoming less effective at supporting discovery. Its institutional implication is to reward independently validated contributions and consequential checking, rather than accelerate paper production and scoring alone.

articles.title: JoVox: Joint Hierarchical Flow Matching for Lightweight Voxel Generation
articles.summary: Generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping their lightweight nature remains an open problem in computer vision. Current generators are either high-fidelity but computationally heavy, or…
articles.abstract: Generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping their lightweight nature remains an open problem in computer vision. Current generators are either high-fidelity but computationally heavy, or lightweight but of lower fidelity. Hierarchical methods keep the lightweight nature of voxels. However, their coarse levels, which decide where all finer cells can appear, are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited, so they are often plausible but wrong. Our key insight is to let finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. To this end, we propose JoVox, a discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the voxel hierarchy, instead of a separate distribution for each level, so that coarse cells can be predicted with finer cells already generated nearby. Within this framework, we further introduce a two-level prediction, which outputs the cells two levels finer at once instead of one level finer, halving the number of levels that the network processes and yielding voxels of higher fidelity. We also introduce an unmasking strategy that revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated and corrects inconsistencies in masked diffusion models. Our framework outperforms the baselines on both unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation. Compared with the current state-of-the-art TRELLIS.2, we achieve 8x higher training throughput, 1/15 of the FLOPs in a forward pass, train on 4 vs. 32 GPUs, and obtain higher quality with an 11% lower Chamfer distance.

articles.title: On the Convergence of First-Order Methods in Signaling Games
articles.summary: We study first-order learning dynamics in Bayesian signaling games, a minimal extensive-form model of strategic interaction under asymmetric information. In these games, a Sender observes a private…
articles.abstract: We study first-order learning dynamics in Bayesian signaling games, a minimal extensive-form model of strategic interaction under asymmetric information. In these games, a Sender observes a private type and chooses a signal, after which a Receiver forms a posterior belief and selects an action. This Bayesian belief update makes the induced learning field fundamentally different from the affine game-gradient fields of normal-form games. Empirically, we find a sharp dichotomy: standard online learning algorithms reliably converge to strict Perfect Bayesian Equilibria (PE), but not to non-strict ones. We show that this behavior cannot be explained by the global geometric conditions commonly used to prove last-iterate convergence, such as monotonicity or the Minty variational inequality. Indeed, these conditions can fail even in binary signaling games. Instead, we identify the relevant local geometry. Our main result characterizes variational stability in finite signaling games: a PE is variationally stable if and only if it is strict. This yields local last-iterate convergence guarantees for online mirror descent and regularized dual averaging near every strict PE. We then study global average-iterate convergence and identify a class of signaling games in which coarse-trigger regret-minimizing dynamics converge to the unique PE. Finally, we complement the theory with experiments comparing projected gradient ascent, mirror-based methods, optimistic variants, and PPO across canonical signaling-game families. The results position signaling games as a compact testbed for understanding how Bayesian belief formation reshapes the convergence geometry of multi-agent learning.

articles.title: A Cooperative Game Theoretic Model for Sustainable, Smallholder Carbon Farming
articles.summary: Carbon farming offers a promising path to improve farmer livelihoods, mitigate climate change, and make farming sustainable. However, smallholder farmers, who dominate agriculture in developing…
articles.abstract: Carbon farming offers a promising path to improve farmer livelihoods, mitigate climate change, and make farming sustainable. However, smallholder farmers, who dominate agriculture in developing economies, face structural barriers to participating in carbon farming due to high certification costs, limited landholdings, and limited budgets available to them. In this paper, we develop a cooperative game-theoretic framework to study how coalition formation can enable viable and profitable participation of smallholder farmers in carbon farming. Our approach explores three components: (i) Solo Portfolio Optimization (SPO), which determines an optimal portfolio of carbon farming practices that individual farmers can adopt under budget constraints; (ii) Joint Portfolio Optimization (JPO), which computes the maximum total economic surplus achievable through the formation of farmer coalitions; and (iii) surplus allocation among participating farmers in a principled way using cooperative game-theoretic solution concepts, such as Shapley value, core, least core, and nucleolus. We show that the underlying cooperative game is superadditive under an affordability condition and non-convex in general. As part of this study, we release CarbonFARM-Bench, a carbon farming dataset constructed by experts, and conduct controlled computational experiments on this dataset. We observe that solo participation in carbon farming is largely infeasible for smallholder farmers under baseline parameters, whereas coalition formation creates substantial value driven by economies of scale. In addition, we demonstrate that stability-aware allocation mechanisms are required for sustaining cooperation. Together, our results highlight that enabling smallholder carbon farming is fundamentally a challenge of institutional design, and we offer several policy recommendations to make it attractive to smallholder farmers.

articles.title: The Power of Two Choices in Dynamic Pricing: As Good As Full Feedback, Instance-Wise
articles.summary: We study the dynamic pricing problem, where a firm sells a product to $T$ myopic customers and their values are independent samples from an unknown value distribution $F$. With posted prices, the…
articles.abstract: We study the dynamic pricing problem, where a firm sells a product to $T$ myopic customers and their values are independent samples from an unknown value distribution $F$. With posted prices, the firm only sees whether each customer buys, and the minimax regret is $\widetilde Θ(T^{2/3})$ [KL03]. A menu instead offers several options, each selling the product with some probability at some expected payment. Infinitely many menu options allow the seller to fully reveal customer values, reducing the regret to $Θ(\sqrt T)$. How many options are needed? Perhaps surprisingly, a second menu option suffices, achieving the same regret as infinite menus (up to $\log$ factors). This holds broadly: without knowing any property of $F$, our algorithm with two menu options attains $\tilde O(\sqrt T)$ regret in general, $\tilde O(T^{1/3})$ regret for monotone-hazard-rate distributions, and $\tilde O(T^{d/(d+1)})$ instance-dependent regret when $d\in(0,1)$ is a suitable notion of "dimension". All are optimal even with infinite menus. Moreover, we argue, via a novel lower-bound construction, that our algorithm is near-optimal for each problem instance. Along the way, we study the query complexity of revenue maximization, where an algorithm issues a query to each customer to learn the property of interest (either the best price or the CDF) up to some precision. We show that interval queries suffice to achieve the same query complexity as value queries (up to $\log$ factors) for both properties and across several classes of value distributions. We provide a new interval-query algorithm for each property. The best-price-estimation algorithm is the key ingredient in our main dynamic pricing algorithm, and the CDF-estimation algorithm underpins a simpler algorithm attaining $\tilde O(\sqrt T)$ regret with three menu options.

articles.title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction
articles.summary: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents.…
articles.abstract: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.

articles.title: Read Less, Solve More: Token-Efficient Sparse Reading of External Content for AI Agents
articles.summary: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading…
articles.abstract: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading increases token and latency costs and can dilute relevant evidence. We present SparseRead, a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model. Its Read Intent Protocol tracks evolving needs and source coverage; Adaptive Reader Backends select how evidence is located and exposed; and the Budgeted Read Gate bounds cumulative raw exposure per episode with faithful full-view fallback. A unified Reader interface supports interchangeable evidence acquisition across heterogeneous resources. Across six models, including Claude Opus 5, and five scenarios, SparseRead reduces total tokens by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, preserving or improving task quality in 97% settings. On Web deep-search tasks, it reduces tokens by 31.0--43.0% and task completion time by 23.0--37.0%. Ablations validate the three designs, while integration with three agent frameworks demonstrates portability.

articles.title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations
articles.summary: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of…
articles.abstract: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.

articles.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
articles.summary: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full…
articles.abstract: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.

articles.title: Test-Time Scaling for Diffusion Language Models with Frequency-Aware Remasking
articles.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies…
articles.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding strategies. Our two-stage approach uses a fast base sampler to solve easy questions, then applies frequency-aware remasking to the remaining hard questions. This strategy tracks how often each token's prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens, encouraging samples to explore alternative reasoning paths rather than collapse onto the model's preferred trajectory. Experiments with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show consistent improvements over a strong adaptive allocation baseline, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 3.73 percentage points (LLaDA) and 7.33 percentage points (Dream) on MATH-500, and absolute coverage gains of up to 11.39 percentage points (LLaDA) and 10.98 percentage points (Dream) on HumanEval. On questions unsolved by the base certainty-aware strategy after 100 samples, frequency-aware remasking recovers solutions for 3.75% to 18.75% of examples.

articles.title: WorldFoundry: Towards Unified Infrastructure for World Intelligence
articles.summary: Visual generative models increasingly blur the line between synthesizing observations and simulating environments. Yet visual plausibility alone does not constitute successful world modeling:…
articles.abstract: Visual generative models increasingly blur the line between synthesizing observations and simulating environments. Yet visual plausibility alone does not constitute successful world modeling: compelling outputs may lack persistent state, physical dynamics, or causally consistent responses to interactions. We define a generative world model as a predictive dynamical system that maintains a persistent, history-conditioned representation of an environment, updates that representation in response to actions or interventions, and generates temporally coherent trajectories that reflect outcomes under observed and counterfactual interventions. From this definition, we derive an intelligence-oriented framework spanning perceptual grounding, persistent state modeling, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction. We present WorldFoundry, open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation across video, 3D and 4D, embodied action, and interactive world systems. WorldFoundry unifies model and benchmark discovery, runtime and asset preparation, execution orchestration, artifact management, and interactive visualization, while modality-specific adapters preserve native inputs, execution semantics, output representations, and evaluation protocols. Explicit manifests, durable artifact contracts, and evidence-aware scorecards separate execution readiness from evaluative claims, making each claim traceable to its supporting artifacts. The catalog contains 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 registered metric entries, with readiness and execution evidence recorded separately. WorldFoundry enables reproducible comparison of persistent, controllable dynamics across heterogeneous systems, advancing the field from perceptual synthesis toward measurable world intelligence.

articles.title: MotionGraphicsBench: Evaluating Motion Graphics Generation with Programmatic Verification
articles.summary: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial,…
articles.abstract: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, compared with 83.3% for a GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline, and outperform the baseline in both approval and rejection recall. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 6.0% to 67.7%. Across 15 models evaluated at their highest available reasoning effort with 32 attempts per instance, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We release our benchmark at https://huggingface.co/datasets/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench.

articles.title: onóna: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings
articles.summary: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output…
articles.abstract: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

articles.title: Energy-Tweedie: Score meets Score, Energy meets Energy
articles.summary: Denoising and score estimation are classically linked through Tweedie's formula, which relates the posterior mean under Gaussian noise to the Stein score of the noisy marginal. In this work, we…
articles.abstract: Denoising and score estimation are classically linked through Tweedie's formula, which relates the posterior mean under Gaussian noise to the Stein score of the noisy marginal. In this work, we extend this perspective beyond Gaussian noise to a broad class of Gibbs (energy-based) noise distributions, with the generalized Gaussian family as an example. We derive the Energy-Tweedie identity: when the denoising posterior is viewed through the lens of scoring rules, the path derivative of a kernel scoring rule defined by the noise potential recovers the Stein score of the noisy marginal. Thus, the familiar correspondence between Gaussian noise, posterior means, squared loss, and Tweedie's formula is lifted to a distributional correspondence between Gibbs noise distributions, full posterior laws, kernel scoring rules, and the Energy-Tweedie identity, which gives a Tweedie-style relation for each noise potential. Among its consequences, this identity gives a posterior-samples-to-score route to score estimation, yields a principled criterion for estimating unknown noise parameters, and enables diffusion-style sampling along user-chosen paths through the noise-parameter space, supplying the score-based perspective on recent generative methods trained with scoring rules.

articles.title: Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning
articles.summary: Learning accurate off-policy state-action value functions (Q-functions) from offline datasets becomes harder as the task horizon grows. One-step temporal-difference (TD) learning bootstraps after…
articles.abstract: Learning accurate off-policy state-action value functions (Q-functions) from offline datasets becomes harder as the task horizon grows. One-step temporal-difference (TD) learning bootstraps after every transition, so small per-step errors accumulate along the horizon, and early states can be badly misvalued even when the TD loss is small. Multi-step TD shortens this chain by following the dataset trajectory for several steps; however, since the behavior policy is often suboptimal, every followed action adds a bias, and no fixed number of steps suits a whole trajectory. In this paper, we propose Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), a simple method that enables accurate long-horizon value learning by automatically balancing between one-step and multi-step returns. HQL extends a target through a dataset action only when the critic values it at least as highly as the best-of-N actions sampled from the BC policy, and otherwise falls back to a one-step target. We show that this rule is a principled off-policy correction that needs no action densities, which makes HQL compatible with expressive flow and diffusion policies. Experiments show that HQL avoids the failures of both one-step and multi-step TD on a combination-lock task across horizons, and outperforms prior horizon-reduction methods on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks.

articles.title: Coding or Cheating? An Investigation of Frontier Coding LLMs
articles.summary: Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving…
articles.abstract: Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving the task. We show that, on hard problems, frontier models often satisfy these rewards by obtaining the answer instead of deriving it, known as reward hacking. Prior reports document this behavior on public benchmarks. We test its persistence on unseen problems. In a hardened environment where the answer cannot leak, nearly every model we tested attempted to recover the answer, escalating through tiers of increasingly specialized exploitation: mining the repository history for the upstream fix, inspecting the git object store directly, and sweeping the filesystem for a possible newer copy of the source or hidden tests. These attempts were concentrated on the hardest problems, and the models differed in whether, how often, and how deeply they escalated. Our position is that this behavior is a learned shortcut, acquired in RL environments that leak the answer, not a sign of intelligence. We release agent traces for these models to support further study at https://huggingface.co/datasets/logitly-ai/reward-hacking-raw-v1.

articles.title: Match the Geometry Before the Surrogate: Extreme Low-Budget Optimization in High Dimensions
articles.summary: Low-budget molecular optimization is often framed as Bayesian optimization in a learned latent space, but standard benchmarks typically allow hundreds or thousands of evaluations, whereas a realistic…
articles.abstract: Low-budget molecular optimization is often framed as Bayesian optimization in a learned latent space, but standard benchmarks typically allow hundreds or thousands of evaluations, whereas a realistic wet-lab round may allow only a few dozen. We revisit this regime using a SELFIES molecular variational autoencoder (VAE) with a Gaussian prior and GuacaMol objectives at N = 30 evaluations. The main finding is not a new surrogate model, but an interaction in candidate generation. The encoder means of a reference set of molecules concentrate near a narrow spherical shell, while many high-dimensional optimizers propose candidates from boxes or box-shaped trust regions. We study a simple constraint, the on-sphere scaffold, that restricts candidate generation to this shell. We then introduce two minimal optimizers to probe what remains useful once the support is fixed. GeoWalk performs geodesic local search on the shell without a surrogate. After 30 evaluations, it shows no detected difference from a Gaussian-process (GP) surrogate on the shell, which is ahead earlier in the budget. GeoCMA adds covariance learning in a random subspace. It does not improve on GeoWalk in the molecular benchmark. On LassoBench it has a lower mean loss than GeoWalk, but full-dimensional CMA-ES remains stronger on most tasks. A factorial experiment with a single GP crosses the candidate support (shell or box) with the acquisition maximizer (a finite candidate set or a continuous optimizer). In this benchmark, shell candidates outperformed box candidates when acquisition was maximized over a candidate set, but not with continuous maximization by L-BFGS-B. These results come from a controlled study of one Gaussian-prior VAE benchmark and do not recommend VAEs for molecular optimization. The practical lesson is to control the candidate support and the acquisition maximizer before attributing a gain to the surrogate.

articles.title: Lower-Level Agnostic Bilevel Optimization
articles.summary: Bilevel optimization is a fundamental framework for machine learning problems, where an upper-level (UL) objective depends on the solution of a nested lower-level (LL) problem. Existing bilevel…
articles.abstract: Bilevel optimization is a fundamental framework for machine learning problems, where an upper-level (UL) objective depends on the solution of a nested lower-level (LL) problem. Existing bilevel algorithms typically assume that the LL objective is available for evaluation, differentiation, or unrolling. However, this assumption can fail when the LL response is produced by a black-box solver, simulator, adversary, or learned predictor. In this paper, we study LL agnostic bilevel optimization, where the UL learner has access only to an approximate LL solution $\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x})$ and cannot query the LL objective, its gradients, Hessian/Jacobian information, or the procedure that generates the LL response. We propose LeGo-BiO, a coordinate-wise pseudo-hypergradient method that estimates the missing Jacobian $\nabla _{\mathbf{x}}\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x})$ using finite differences of $\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\cdot)$. For each UL coordinate, LeGo-BiO constructs a decision vector subject to 1-sparse updates, thereby isolating the corresponding Jacobian column needed in the UL gradient computation. This avoids the directional-projection limitation of full-parameter response differences and, unlike derivative-free/zeroth-order approximations of the entire UL gradient, preserves the available first-order gradient information with respect to the UL variables for more accurate UL gradient evaluation. We establish convergence guarantees for LeGo-BiO in both deterministic and stochastic settings under an LL error-bound/Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type condition, without requiring LL strong convexity. Our bounds yield an $O(T^{-1})$ rate in the deterministic setting and an $O(T^{-1/2})$ rate in the stochastic setting when the LL approximation error decreases geometrically. Experiments demonstrate competitive performance of LeGo-BiO despite being agnostic to the LL objective.

articles.title: Quasipolynomial-Time Planning for Decodable POMDPs
articles.summary: We study planning for finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with finite state, action, and observation spaces. Both exact and approximate planning are known to be…
articles.abstract: We study planning for finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with finite state, action, and observation spaces. Both exact and approximate planning are known to be computationally hard in this setting, so prior work has explored natural assumptions that make planning easier. Recent work [Golowich et al., 2022] gave quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for observable POMDPs. These are POMDPs whose observation channels satisfy an $\ell_1$-observability condition, but notably, no assumptions are required on the transition dynamics. In a similar vein, for every fixed $ρ>0$, we give quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for $ρ$-decodable POMDPs. We show that decodability is implied by both $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-observability and is strictly weaker than observability. Moreover, we show that the optimal decodability constant can be computed in polynomial time, whereas computing the optimal $\ell_1$-observability constant is NP-hard in the worst case. We also show that the fast filter-forgetting guarantee underlying the approach of [Golowich et al., 2022] does not extend directly from $\ell_1$-observability to constant $\ell_2$-observability. Thus, decodability is an easy-to-check, unifying assumption under which quasipolynomial-time approximate planning for POMDPs is possible.

articles.title: Adaptive Budgeted Data Acquisition for Robust Off-Policy Evaluation from Multiple Loggers
